title: Fact check: Fire in Riga is not linked to drone production for Ukraine “in the heart of the city”
content:
The claims appear to be aimed at fuelling negative sentiment towards Latvia’s defence and military industry. However, both the company mentioned in the posts and Latvia’s drone manufacturers’ association have confirmed that neither the building nor the fire had any connection to companies manufacturing unmanned aerial vehicles.

On Wednesday, a TikTok account called “separatistlv”, known for spreading pro-Kremlin propaganda, published a video showing the massive plume of smoke rising above the burning building. Accompanied by dramatic music, the video included the following caption in Russian: “One of the warehouses storing components for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), which Latvia was supposed to send to Ukraine, is burning. Let’s get the job done, brothers.” The short video has attracted nearly half a million views.

This was not the only example. Similar rumours, allegedly based on “what people are saying in the comments”, were spread on TikTok by another man, who claimed that the address housed Edge Autonomy, a company manufacturing drones.

title: Will ketchup in EU restaurants have to be served only from communal bottles?
content:
An EU decision does provide for a ban on certain types of single-use plastic packaging, and these restrictions will take effect in 2030. However, the changes do not require diners to use communal bottles or refillable dispensers specifically.

A post circulating on the social media platform X states that “the EU is banning single-use plastic sachets for ketchup and other sauces — from now on, customers will have to use communal bottles or refillable dispensers.” The post is illustrated with images of European Commission (EC) President Ursula von der Leyen and a small ketchup sachet.

The post quickly gained popularity. It was accompanied by many unflattering comments: “Ethnic cleansing is taking place across the continent, while the idiots in Brussels are worried about ketchup sachets”; “Everything is fine, the world has been saved, and so has the climate. Next, they should regulate how large the eye of a needle must be for threading”; “The EU sometimes reminds me of a situation where you really, really, really ought to be studying, but instead you organise your sock drawer just so you can feel that you have at least done something useful”; and others.

title: “Harmony Centre’s” parliamentary candidate calls for Latvia to leave NATO
content:
To justify his position, the politician relied on a series of false claims that suggest either a lack of understanding or a deliberate distortion of facts. Nevertheless, his Facebook post received several hundred supportive reactions and comments, while nearly a hundred users shared it further.

After reviewing Aleksejs Vasiļjevs ‘ post, Jānis Sārts, Director of the NATO Strategic Communications Centre of Excellence (StratCom), told Delfi that everyone is entitled to their opinion, but opinions should be based on facts, logic and cause-and-effect relationships. According to him, Vasiļjevs’ publication lacks all three. “When people fail to do that, I see it either as a conspiracy-based worldview or as an attempt to spread narratives favourable to Russia,“ the expert concluded.

Since the politician structured his arguments point by point, we will address them in the same order.

At the beginning of his post, Vasiļjevs complains that when Latvia joined NATO in 2004, the country was promised security, yet today children and grandchildren are being sent into school basements whenever another drone alert is issued. “In the beginning, there were no alerts at all,” the politician claims.

title: Baltic military technology companies attract major funding as Latvia seeks to catch up with its neighbours
content:
At present, most of the capital raised is still flowing into Estonia, although both the number of companies and the volume of investment are growing rapidly in Latvia and Lithuania as well. Industry representatives believe that further breakthroughs will depend on access to funding for early-stage companies and on how quickly innovations can be integrated into practical applications.

Start-ups operating in the defence, security, and resilience sectors in the Baltic States raised 104 million euros last year, according to the latest Baltic deep-tech review, the Baltic Deep Tech Report 2025, prepared by the Baltic-based venture capital fund Iron Wolf Capital.

This amount accounted for 15.4% of all funding raised by companies in 2025. The report also notes that investment attracted by the defence and security sector is often systematically underreported, meaning that the actual volume of investment may be even higher.

Baltic companies that completed the largest funding rounds:

  •  Blackwall — 45 million euros;
  • PowerUP Energy Technologies — 10 million euros;
  • Lendurai — 5.5 million euros;
  • Wayren — 7.9 million US dollars;
  • Skeleton Technologies — 7 million US dollars;
  • Elcogen — 5 million euros;

title: Not for nothing they are called the “Bloodlands”: how to understand the Polish-Ukrainian “order scandal”?
content:
The Ukrainians did not leave the move unanswered: in solidarity with their president, several prominent Ukrainian figures returned their Polish state decorations and senior Ukrainian officials declined to attend a conference of particular importance to Poland.

However, Armands Astukevičs, a researcher at the Centre for East European Policy Studies, argues in an interview with Delfi that the controversy is better explained by Poland’s domestic political manoeuvring, namely the president’s desire to undermine the prime minister. Meanwhile, historian Valdis Kuzmins, a researcher at the Latvian National Defence Academy, notes that finding a simple answer as to which side in the cycle of nationalist violence during the Second World War was the “good” one that harmed no one is virtually an impossible task.

title: Romanian Defence Ministry debunks false claim about alleged Russian inspections of military bases in Romania
content:
In a Facebook post, the retired general argued that, “under the Treaty on Conventional Armed Forces in Europe (CFE Treaty), Romania had been required to provide all signatory states, including Russia, with annual detailed information on the number and location of key categories of military equipment”.

He further claimed that, before Romania suspended its participation in the treaty in 2023, Russian military inspection teams had physically entered Romanian bases and depots to verify that the country remained within the treaty’s limits.

He also stated that, during his time as a commander, he personally received an unannounced Russian inspection conducted under the OSCE’s Vienna Document mechanism. According to his account, Romania’s Defence Ministry annually submitted data on the structure of the armed forces, active military personnel and newly acquired major weapons systems, including the first F-16 fighter jets and HIMARS launchers.

The Romanian Defence Ministry responded through its Inforadar platform, explaining in detail why these claims are misleading and factually incorrect.

title: Pragmatism and respect for existing alliances — this is how Bulgaria will now support Ukraine
content:
The Coalition of the Willing is an informal multilateral structure created as a European mechanism for supporting Ukraine, led by France and the United Kingdom. It brings together nearly 40 countries in a broad political format, but the actual military planning is carried out by nine member states that undertake specific military commitments.

Bulgaria — and more specifically Prime Minister Rumen Radev — officially declined the invitation to join this coalition, arguing that the country does not take part in formats that insist on continued financial and military assistance which it is not in a position to provide. This stance is often interpreted as a refusal of solidarity. In this case, however, Bulgaria justified its decision by its determination to adhere strictly to the established frameworks of the EU and NATO.

title: How China bypasses new tariffs: Temu and Shein change strategy
content:
Cheap shopping from China is a phenomenon that has accompanied European consumers for years, but has recently intensified. With the acceleration of global trade connections, ordinary citizens began to mass-purchase cheap, often questionable-quality products from giants like AliExpress, Shein, or Temu. Consumers primarily experience the benefits in the form of low prices for home appliances and accessories. 

This phenomenon relies on the “wow” effect: access to a massive, virtual store where almost everything can be bought cheaper than in physical brick-and-mortar stores. In the long run, however, these products usually turn out to be of such poor quality that their usefulness does not exceed a few months, and they often end up in the trash almost immediately after unpacking, exacerbating the problem of environmental pollution.

title: Parents or Big Tech? Who should be responsible for children online?
content:
A report by the Special Panel on Child Safety Online, established by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, leaves little room for doubt: the current social media model is failing to provide children with adequate protection.

The findings reinforce what researchers have been warning for years. Social media platforms are deliberately designed to maximize users’ attention, relying on addictive design features, algorithmic personalization, and endless scrolling to keep people engaged for as long as possible.

The report also highlights persistent problems, including minors’ easy access to harmful content, ineffective age verification, and a system that places too much responsibility for children’s online safety on parents.

The experts argue that online platforms—not families—should bear primary responsibility for creating a safe digital environment for children. In their view, parental controls alone cannot serve as the foundation of child protection.

title: The Teutonic Knights: The forgotten order connecting Europe’s East and West
content:
In the broader Western consciousness, the Teutonic Knights are largely stripped of their specific geography. They are loosely lumped together with the Templars and Hospitallers into a single, romanticised pop-culture trope: the generic medieval Crusader. 

For the average Western European, the colour of the cross on the cloak – black, red, or white – is a distinction lost to time. Even in Germany, awareness of the Order has faded into a niche historical footnote.

For Poles, Lithuanians, and some other Eastern European nations, however, the Teutonic Knights evoke an entirely different category of historical memory. They are not distant holy warriors, but the skilled architects of a powerful, militarised monastic state carved out along the Baltic coast.

title: NATO’s eastward expansion explained: How Russia’s words helped convince a hesitant America
content:
Pro-Kremlin propaganda has long claimed that NATO broke an alleged promise not to expand eastward. Vladimir Putin himself invoked this narrative to justify Russia’s actions on the eve of the invasion of Ukraine: “There were promises to our country not to expand NATO even one inch to the east. I repeat – they deceived us, in other words, they simply conned us.”

Politicians sympathetic to Moscow – including some in Slovakia – have echoed this version of events. “The Russians are right. The West repeatedly deceived them, for example over NATO enlargement. Russia is now fighting for its security guarantees,” the Slovak prime minister Robert Fico once said in an interview with the controversial Slovak outlet Hlavné správy.

Historians and security experts have repeatedly debunked this claim, pointing out that no written agreement of this kind was ever signed. This was later confirmed by the first and last president of the Soviet Union, Mikhail Gorbachev.

A deeper perspective on these events comes from the prominent American diplomat Ronald D. Asmus, one of the architects of NATO enlargement and a key adviser to former U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.

title: Below the Threshold: How Russia Is Testing NATO Without Starting a War
content:
Kevin Riehle spent more than three decades working in US national security and now lectures on intelligence and security at Brunel University of London. His specialist field is Russian intelligence services and covert operations — the institutions and methods operating between routine espionage and open war.

When Russian drones or military aircraft enter or approach NATO airspace, he says, the immediate purpose may be reconnaissance: measuring detection times, identifying which institutions respond and observing how political leaders describe the incident.

“Essentially, Russia is testing the boundaries,” Riehle says. It wants to discover not only what NATO can detect, but what it will tolerate. The question is when the Alliance decides that enough is enough.

Russia has long cast itself as the injured or encircled party rather than the aggressor. A forceful response to a limited airspace violation could therefore be absorbed into the Kremlin’s narrative that NATO started the confrontation.

title: €23 Billion and the ETS Dispute: Who Is Really Responsible for High Energy Bills?
content:
The intellectual foundations of emissions trading date back to the 1960s and Ronald Coase’s landmark paper The Problem of Social Cost. Coase argued that clearly defined and properly priced property rights would allow market forces to reflect the true cost of environmental damage, provided governments established and enforced rights to use environmental resources.

The theory was first put into practice in the United States in the 1990s through the Acid Rain Program, an emissions trading scheme targeting sulfur dioxide. The results were striking: sulfur dioxide emissions fell by 95 percent. The program’s success convinced the signatories of the 1997 Kyoto Protocol to adopt tradable emission permits as a cornerstone of global climate policy. The protocol embraced emissions trading and flexible mechanisms as cost-effective tools for reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

title: Maria Skłodowska-Curie on the New Euro Banknote: Voting Open to Everyone
content:
Money has always been more than just a tool to facilitate everyday transactions. It is a powerful carrier of identity, a miniature history lesson, and a calling card that millions of people carry in their wallets every day. After more than twenty years of the European currency functioning in its unchanged, familiar form, the time has come for one of the greatest metamorphoses in the history of EU finances. 

The European Central Bank has just placed the decision on what the entirely new series of banknotes will look like in the hands of citizens. There is not much time, as the digital ballot boxes close on September 21, 2026. Most importantly, however, this historic vote is not reserved exclusively for countries using the common currency. 

Although the official eurozone currently includes twenty-one countries, the EU money permeates borders, constituting an integral part of life across the continent. We use it during holiday travels, international business transactions, and cross-border trade. For this reason, the European Central Bank made the unprecedented decision to open the consultations to all residents of Europe.

title: What is the digital euro and how will it work?
content:
The digital euro (eEUR) is a new initiative of the European Union. Under the current plan, starting in 2029 the euro area is to have an additional means of payment – one that functions exactly like cash, but without a physical form.

Work on the project has been underway since 2021, when the exploratory phase began. However, progress accelerated only recently.

In December 2025, the EU Member States in the Council of the European Union agreed on the project’s basic principles: the digital currency may only complement cash. At the same time, it is intended to be available anytime and anywhere to both individuals and businesses.

This marked the beginning of the next stage of preparations. Its objective is to establish the infrastructure required for the future rollout of the new currency, cooperation with private-sector partners, and an appropriate legal framework.

Partners have already been selected – around 36 companies from the financial sector that qualified for the ECB Innovation Platform programme. The list includes organisations such as Revolut, Stripe, UniCredit, and Deutsche Bank. Together, they are expected to work on ensuring technical readiness.

In recent days, claims have spread in the Czech public debate that the European Union is seeking to ban the Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN) party simply because it holds different political views from most other parties.

title: Lithuania outpaces many NATO members: expert explains what is driving this breakthrough
content:
Official NATO data show that countries are progressing toward this new target at very different speeds. While the Baltic states and Poland have already reached – or are close to reaching – it, many other countries are advancing much more slowly. Experts emphasize that differences in the share of GDP allocated to defence are determined not only by countries’ economic capabilities, but also by how they assess the threat posed by Russia and by the extent of political consensus on defence priorities.

NATO comprises 32 member states: the United States, Canada, and 30 European countries. In recent years, a number of NATO allies have steadily increased their defence spending. This trend has been driven both by the threat posed by Russia and by pressure from the United States for its European allies to take greater responsibility for their own security.

title: As Drought Returns and Another Heatwave Approaches, Hungary Has Decided to Take Action
content:
The new Hungarian government had not even been formed when, in early May, László Gajdos, who was appointed Minister responsible for the Living Environment shortly afterwards, asked the public not to mow their lawns that month. Besides the fact that uncut grass and wildflowers sequester carbon dioxide, while the latter also support pollinators, one reason for the initiative was that Hungary was experiencing an exceptional drought at the time: April this year was the driest since 1901, and in early May, at the height of the drought, half of the country was affected by a high level of drought and the other half by severe drought.

Not mowing the grass is a very simple, almost trivial measure: soil beneath cut grass dries out more quickly, while the grass itself is scorched and has to be watered more frequently, leading to additional water consumption. If the grass is allowed to grow longer, it provides better cover for the soil, making it more difficult for the soil to dry out. However, the fact that László Gajdos had to draw particular attention to this shows that a change in mindset is needed – and not only when it comes to mowing grass.
